files.model.yaml:
model: observability
title: An observability platform — metrics, logs and traces
currency: USD

description: >-
  The book's second model, and the counterweight to the web service. Three multiplicative
  chains hang off the same few roots, so they are correlated whether or not anybody says so; label
  cardinality is a product of uncertain counts and therefore dominates everything downstream of
  it; the control knobs are sampling and retention rather than money; and there are three separate
  outputs with three separate ceilings, which no single number can summarise.

  It also has a hole in it. Spans per request is a property of somebody's instrumented
  application, not of any corpus or any machine, so this repository cannot measure it — and the
  whole traces chain is therefore shown as unmeasured rather than filled in with a plausible
  number. That is not a gap waiting to be tidied up. It is what an honest sizing model looks like
  before the measurement is taken, and it is on a published page for exactly that reason.

nodes:

  # -- shared roots ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Everything below flows from these five. That is what makes the three chains correlated by
  # construction: they are not three models, they are one estate seen three ways.

  hosts:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: host
    value: 1200
    note: >-
      No band: an estate is a thing you can count, and this one has been counted. What it does
      next is growth_factor's business, not this node's.
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "stated estate size (ch02)"}
    range: [50, 3000]

  request_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: request/second
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 8000.0, likely: 25000.0, maximum: 90000.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch03 — the busy hour across the estate, not the daily mean. Triangular: a
        minimum, a likely and a maximum is the whole of what a dashboard gives you, and the
        maximum is the busiest hour anybody has looked at rather than the busiest one there
        will be"
    range: [2000, 200000]

  annual_growth:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 1.15, p90: 1.70}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch04 — telemetry grows faster than the traffic it describes, because teams add
        instrumentation as well as load. Lognormal like any growth rate — it compounds and
        cannot go negative — and wider than the web service's for the same reason its
        median is higher"

  horizon:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: year
    value: 3
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the planning horizon for this platform"}
    range: [1, 5]

  one_year:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: year
    value: 1
    note: "as in the web service model: an exponent has to be a pure number"
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  horizon_periods:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: horizon / one_year

  growth_factor:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    formula: annual_growth ** horizon_periods

  # -- label cardinality: the combinatorial node ------------------------------------------------

  label_values_endpoint:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 6.0, maximum: 20.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "distinct routes appearing as a label value. Triangular because somebody could
        go and count them this afternoon; the maximum is the routes that exist today, and a
        new service adds to it"

  label_values_status:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 3.0, maximum: 6.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "distinct status classes kept as a label. Triangular, and the one input in this
        model whose bounds are genuinely hard: a request cannot carry a status the code does
        not emit"

  label_values_accidental:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: dimensionless
    label: accidental label values
    note: >-
      The label nobody planned. A pod name under a rolling deploy, a customer id added during an
      incident, a version string. Lognormal and wide, because the failure mode is multiplicative:
      whatever it is, it multiplies every series that carries it, and the distribution has to be
      able to express "usually nothing, occasionally catastrophic".
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 1.0, p90: 6.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "ch08 — the cardinality explosion, as a distribution rather than as a warning.
        Lognormal because this one has no ceiling: a label carrying a user id multiplies the
        series count by a number nobody chose, and a triangular would assert a maximum that
        does not exist"

  label_cardinality:
    kind: derived
    unit: dimensionless
    label: label cardinality
    note: >-
      A product of uncertain counts, which is why it is lognormal-ish whether or not anybody chose
      that, and why it dominates the tornado for every metrics figure in this model. Multiplying
      three quantities that are each uncertain by a factor of three gives one uncertain by a
      factor of twenty-seven, and no amount of care about the other inputs recovers that.
    formula: label_values_endpoint * label_values_status * label_values_accidental

  # -- chain one: metrics ------------------------------------------------------------------------

  base_metrics_per_host:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: series/host
    value: 60
    label: metric names per host
    note: >-
      No band: scrape one host and list them. The uncertainty in this chain is what the labels
      multiply that list by, and label_cardinality carries it.
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "distinct metric names exposed per host, before labels"}
    range: [10, 400]

  active_series:
    kind: derived
    unit: series
    formula: hosts * base_metrics_per_host * label_cardinality * growth_factor

  scrape_interval:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: second
    value: 30
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12): doubling it halves the metrics
      chain and loses resolution that cannot be recovered afterwards"}
    range: [10, 120]

  one_sample_per_series:
    kind: input
    decided: definition
    unit: sample/series
    value: 1
    note: "one scrape takes one sample from one series. A rate is a count over a duration, and the
      count needs a unit before the division means anything"
    provenance: {kind: fact, source: "definition"}

  sample_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: sample/series/second
    formula: one_sample_per_series / scrape_interval

  metrics_sample_bytes:
    kind: measured
    unit: byte/sample
    label: bytes per sample, compressed
    result: metrics-sample-bytes

  metrics_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: metrics ingest
    formula: active_series * sample_rate * metrics_sample_bytes

  metrics_retention:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: day
    value: 400
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12)"}
    range: [15, 800]

  metrics_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: metrics_ingest * metrics_retention

  # -- chain two: logs ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  lines_per_request:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: line/request
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 3.0, likely: 9.0, maximum: 30.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "application log lines emitted per request served. Triangular, from reading a
        sample of the logs — and the maximum is the part to distrust, because a debug flag
        left on in production is outside it"

  log_keep_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 1.0
    label: fraction of log lines kept
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12): drop and aggregation rules"}
    range: [0.05, 1.0]

  log_line_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: line/second
    formula: request_rate * lines_per_request * log_keep_rate * growth_factor

  logs_line_bytes:
    kind: measured
    unit: byte/line
    label: bytes per log line, compressed
    result: logs-line-bytes

  logs_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: logs ingest
    formula: log_line_rate * logs_line_bytes

  logs_retention:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: day
    value: 30
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12)"}
    range: [3, 365]

  logs_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: logs_ingest * logs_retention

  # -- chain three: traces, and the constant nobody has measured ------------------------------------

  spans_per_request:
    kind: measured
    unit: span/request
    label: spans per request
    note: >-
      Not measurable from anything in this repository. It is a property of one instrumented
      application at one version, so it belongs to the `estate` target — an observation somebody
      takes of a system they run, disclosed rather than verified (ch03). Until somebody takes it,
      every figure below is absent rather than estimated.
    result: traces-spans-per-request

  trace_keep_rate:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: dimensionless
    value: 0.05
    label: trace sampling rate
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12), and the one with the widest
      range: head sampling at 1% and at 100% are two different platforms"}
    range: [0.001, 1.0]

  span_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: span/second
    formula: request_rate * spans_per_request * trace_keep_rate * growth_factor

  traces_span_bytes:
    kind: measured
    unit: byte/span
    label: bytes per span, compressed
    result: traces-span-bytes

  traces_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: traces ingest
    formula: span_rate * traces_span_bytes

  traces_retention:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: day
    value: 14
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "a control knob (ch12)"}
    range: [1, 90]

  traces_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: traces_ingest * traces_retention

  # -- output one: the ingest pipeline ---------------------------------------------------------------

  known_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    label: ingest, metrics and logs only
    note: >-
      Metrics plus logs, and deliberately *not* the total. It is a lower bound with a whole chain
      missing from it, and ch19 is about exactly this shape of error: a number that is correct
      arithmetic over an incomplete structure looks identical to a number that is right.
    formula: metrics_ingest + logs_ingest

  total_ingest:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    formula: metrics_ingest + logs_ingest + traces_ingest

  collector_cores:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: core
    value: 16
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the sizing decision for the ingest tier"}
    range: [8, 512]

  collector_throughput_quoted:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: MB/s/core
    value: 6
    note: >-
      No band, and giving a quote one would be inventing a range nobody quoted. A vendor states a
      single number; the spread belongs to the measurement, and collector_throughput_measured
      below carries it with a standard error.
    provenance:
      kind: vendor_claim
      source: "throughput per core as documented by the collector. Unverified here, and marked as
        a claim in every figure it appears in"

  collector_throughput_measured:
    kind: measured
    unit: MB/s/core
    label: collector throughput per core, measured
    note: >-
      The same quantity as the node above, taken rather than quoted. It needs the reference
      machine (`rig`) and nobody has run it, so the ceiling built on it is absent while the
      ceiling built on the vendor's claim is not. Reading those two rows next to each other is
      most of ch03.
    result: collector-throughput-per-core

  quoted_pipeline_capacity:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    formula: collector_cores * collector_throughput_quoted

  measured_pipeline_capacity:
    kind: derived
    unit: MB/s
    formula: collector_cores * collector_throughput_measured

  quoted_pipeline_utilisation:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: ingest utilisation, quoted
    of: known_ingest / quoted_pipeline_capacity
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.4
    because: >-
      A queueing ceiling, not a capacity one (ch06), so the margin is large: a pipeline at 80% of
      quoted throughput has a queue in front of it, and a queue in front of an ingest pipeline is
      dropped telemetry exactly when something is going wrong. Understated twice over — the
      numerator excludes traces and the denominator is a vendor's claim.

  pipeline_utilisation:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: ingest utilisation, measured
    of: total_ingest / measured_pipeline_capacity
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.4
    because: >-
      The honest version of the row above, and it cannot be computed. Both halves are missing a
      measurement, which is the correct output of this model today.

  # -- output two: the retention store -----------------------------------------------------------

  usable_tb_per_node:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: TB/node
    value: 40
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "usable capacity per storage node after replication"}
    range: [20, 400]

  store_nodes:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: node
    value: 12
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the sizing decision for the retention tier"}
    range: [5, 400]

  installed_usable:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    formula: store_nodes * usable_tb_per_node

  known_stored:
    kind: derived
    unit: TB
    label: stored, metrics and logs only
    formula: metrics_stored + logs_stored

  store_fill:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: retention store fill
    of: known_stored / installed_usable
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.3
    because: >-
      Capacity, with a rebuild reserve (ch11) — and again a lower bound, because the traces chain
      is not in the numerator. A verdict of `ok` here means "ok, ignoring traces", which is a
      different claim and one the reader should be made to notice.

  # -- output three: the query path -----------------------------------------------------------------

  queries_per_second:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: query/second
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 2.0, likely: 12.0, maximum: 60.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "dashboards, alert rules and people, at the busy hour. Triangular because two of
        those three are countable and the third is not"

  series_per_query_base:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: series/query
    label: series per query, before labels
    distribution: {triangular: {minimum: 40.0, likely: 300.0, maximum: 2000.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "how many distinct metric-name-and-host combinations one dashboard panel or alert
        rule covers, before any label expansion. Triangular, and wide: dashboards differ from
        each other more than anything else in this model does"

  series_per_query:
    kind: derived
    unit: series/query
    note: >-
      The same cardinality node that drives the metrics ingest chain drives this one too, by a
      different route: a label that multiplies the series a scrape produces also multiplies the
      series a query has to walk past to ignore. That is why one accidental label breaks two
      ceilings at once, and why turning down scrape interval and retention — which fix the first
      — does nothing at all for the second (ch12).
    formula: series_per_query_base * label_cardinality

  query_series_rate:
    kind: derived
    unit: series/second
    formula: queries_per_second * series_per_query

  query_nodes:
    kind: input
    decided: you
    unit: node
    value: 24
    provenance: {kind: assumption, source: "the sizing decision for the query tier"}
    range: [2, 120]

  query_scan_rate_quoted:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: series/second/node
    value: 90000
    note: >-
      No band, for the same reason as the collector's quoted throughput: a quote is one number,
      and widening it here would put a range in the vendor's mouth. Nobody has measured this one,
      so nothing in this model disputes it yet.
    provenance: {kind: vendor_claim, source: "series scanned per second per query node, quoted"}

  query_capacity:
    kind: derived
    unit: series/second
    formula: query_nodes * query_scan_rate_quoted

  query_utilisation:
    kind: ceiling
    unit: dimensionless
    label: query path utilisation
    of: query_series_rate / query_capacity
    limit: 1
    headroom: 0.4
    because: >-
      Queueing again, and the tier where a breach is most visible: a dashboard that times out
      during an incident is the failure people remember. Cardinality feeds this and the ingest
      ceiling by different routes, so a single accidental label breaks both at once.

  # -- a small cost tail ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  storage_price:
    kind: input
    decided: outside
    unit: USD/TB/month
    distribution: {lognormal: {p10: 9.0, p90: 24.0}}
    provenance:
      kind: assumption
      source: "all-in cost of a usable TB-month on this tier. Lognormal because it is a price —
        and carried across by hand from whichever storage tier's unit economics somebody had to
        hand, rather than by sampling, which is the seam ch18 is about"

  known_storage_cost:
    kind: derived
    unit: USD/month
    label: retention cost, metrics and logs only
    formula: known_stored * storage_price

outputs:
  - metrics_ingest
  - logs_ingest
  - traces_ingest
  - traces_stored
  - known_ingest
  - known_stored
  - active_series
  - label_cardinality
  - known_storage_cost
  - store_fill
  - quoted_pipeline_utilisation
  - query_utilisation
  - pipeline_utilisation

correlations:
  - a: annual_growth
    b: label_values_accidental
    rho: 0.5
    because: >-
      A platform that is growing is a platform that is being changed, and labels arrive with
      changes. Treating the two as independent makes the metrics interval narrower than the
      estate warrants — ch14 measures by how much.

  - a: request_rate
    b: lines_per_request
    rho: 0.3
    because: >-
      Weak and positive: busier services tend to be the chattier ones. Small enough to be worth
      including as an example of a correlation that barely matters, which is a useful thing for a
      reader to see beside one that does.

  - a: request_rate
    b: queries_per_second
    rho: 0.4
    because: >-
      A busier platform is one more people are watching. Moderate rather than strong: most query
      load comes from alert rules and dashboards on timers, which do not care how busy anything
      is — right up until an incident, when they all fire at once and nobody is looking at the
      model.
files.scenarios/knobs_turned_down.yaml:
scenario: knobs_turned_down
title: The four knobs, turned down
because: >-
  The same estate with every control knob moved: 60-second scrapes, 90-day metric retention, a
  tenth of the log lines kept, and 1% trace sampling. Here so that ch12 can put a number on what
  each knob buys — and so the reader can see that the knobs do not touch cardinality at all,
  which is the input that dominates everything.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides:
  scrape_interval: 60
  metrics_retention: 90
  log_keep_rate: 0.1
  trace_keep_rate: 0.01
files.scenarios/reference.yaml:
scenario: reference
title: Reference scenario
because: >-
  The platform as declared: 30-second scrapes, 400-day metric retention, 30-day logs, 5% trace
  sampling. Every figure the book quotes for this model comes from here unless it says otherwise.
samples: 100000
seed: 20260916
overrides: {}

correlations.because: A platform that is growing is a platform that is being changed, and labels arrive with changes. Treating the two as independent makes the metrics interval narrower than the estate warrants — ch14 measures by how much.

Weak and positive: busier services tend to be the chattier ones. Small enough to be worth including as an example of a correlation that barely matters, which is a useful thing for a reader to see beside one that does.

A busier platform is one more people are watching. Moderate rather than strong: most query load comes from alert rules and dashboards on timers, which do not care how busy anything is — right up until an incident, when they all fire at once and nobody is looking at the model.
